Hi Lauren — thanks for the clear list. Answering each point below with specifics and a couple of caveats. Looping in Monica and Marissa for Dedicated/private deployment nuances and export ops.

Short answers (tl;dr):
- Retention defaults: hosted = 90 days for access logs, 365 days for audit logs (configurable via plan); Dedicated = configurable by contract (typically 1–5 years); Private = fully customer-controlled. 
- Tombstones: we maintain tombstone markers for deletions in the audit stream for 30 days post-delete to support reconciliation; raw event payloads are removed per retention policy.
- Export formats: NDJSON and parquet are supported natively; CSV is available for access-log summaries. Exports are chunked (configurable window) and accompanied by a manifest with SHA256 checksums.
- Retention changes: retroactive policy changes trigger an administrative erase workflow (see steps below) and we can produce a deletion attestment for exported artifacts.
- Delivery: yes — for EU residency we can push exports directly to customer S3 buckets in the region using a short‑lived presigned URL or a push to a customer-managed bucket; links are time-limited (default 72 hours) and we recommend pull‑to‑customer S3 to avoid cross-border transfer logs.

Details and runbook pointers:
1) Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private
  - Hosted: default windows above; customers can request extended retention via Dedicated upgrade or add-on. For hosted tenants we enforce multi-tenant encryption keys; exports are delivered via presigned S3 links or secure FTP depending on compliance needs.
  - Dedicated: retention windows are set in the SLA and enforced by the tenant controller; we keep a short system audit trail of administrative actions for 1 year by default.
  - Private: full control — customer KMS and retention enforcement; Redwood provides export tooling and a support runbook.

2) Export packaging and manifest
  - Supported formats: newline-delimited JSON (events), parquet (columnar for analytics), CSV for summarized access records.
  - Chunking: exports are created in time-bounded chunks (configurable) — common patterns: 7d, 30d, monthly.
  - Manifest: every export set includes manifest.json with per-file SHA256, size, record count, start/end timestamps, and schema version. See attached sample manifest (export_manifest_sample.json).

3) Deletion and legal hold behavior
  - Retention rollback: if you shorten a retention window, we will only delete events that exceed the new window after the change; if you lengthen it, nothing is restored.
  - Retroactive erase (legal/subject access): we follow this flow:
    a) Customer raises an erase/export request with unique request id.
    b) Ops generates export chunks for the requested scope and fingerprints (manifest).
    c) If deletion is requested, we mark tombstone entries and run background purge jobs that remove payloads and update the manifest with deletion flags.
    d) We provide an attestation PDF (signed) showing which files were deleted and the SHA256 of the deleted artifacts prior to purge.
  - Note: tombstones are retained for 30 days to support dispute/reconciliation; after that tombstones are also removed per policy unless a legal hold is present.

4) Residency and delivery
  - We can deliver to customer S3 in-region using push (recommended) or provide presigned GET links (72h default).
  - For cross-border regulatory concerns we offer an encrypted envelope flow: exports are encrypted with a customer public key and only the customer can unwrap them, reducing transfer risk.

Known edge cases (important)
  - Out-of-order events: we include a sequence id and ingestion timestamp; exports are sorted by ingestion timestamp but include original event_time to preserve order where it matters.
  - Partial retention across chunk boundaries: we include boundary markers in the manifest and, when requested, can produce partial-file proofs (hash ranges).
  - PII redaction: we do not redact logs by default; if you need redaction we recommend pre-export transform jobs (we can assist with patterns). Redaction changes hashable content — manifest reflects transformed files.

Runbook / Next steps for Aureum:
  - If you want a 2y legal hold for a subset of users, please send: a) list of user IDs; b) target tenant id; c) hold start/end dates. We will create a hold id and provide a monitoring URL.
  - For an emergency snapshot request, we can stand up a priority export (48–72h SLA) after a legal/POA is signed.

Attaching a sample manifest and a short presigned-link text file for reference. Let us know if you want us to prepare a staged export to your EU S3 for verification.

Adding a couple of technical clarifications from infra/reliability:

- Export consistency: exports are generated from immutable snapshot points in the partitioned log store. We guarantee per-partition monotonicity and include sequence ids in the manifest to help reconcile consumer processing.
- Tombstone semantics: tombstones are a lightweight record that include original record SHA256, deletion timestamp and reason code (user_requested/system_purge/legal_hold). The tombstone payload is not the original event — it is a pointer/marker.
- Export replay and replayability: If you need to replay events into a downstream analytics cluster, parquet chunks include schema vX and partition keys; NDJSON is the canonical event dump.

If Aureum intends to keep exported data in a separate analytics pipeline, we'll recommend parquet + partitioning by month for efficient re-ingest.

Rishi
Senior Infrastructure Engineer, Redwood Inference
